subsection: 4. Africa and the “winds of change”: Algeria and de Gaulle

notes.b: After the Second World War the old empires were harder to hold than before. Britain and France had to decide whether to fight for their colonies or let them go, and France's own recent history shaped its choices.
points: Empires lost both the power and the will to continue: war-weariness at home, the weakness of Britain and France after the war, and hostility to empire from both the United States and the Soviet Union all made colonial rule harder to defend.

The new United Nations gave colonial peoples a public place to raise their grievances, and nationalist movements (organised groups demanding self-rule) grew stronger, so every colony became a potential problem for its ruler.

France was defeated in 1940 and the Vichy regime governed France afterwards, which damaged French prestige. De Gaulle's appeal of 18 June 1940, made from London, began the Free French movement that fought on.
The Fourth Republic (1946–58) was unstable, with weak governments that rarely lasted long, so France found it hard to settle on a firm colonial policy.
Britain's withdrawal from India in 1947 and France's defeat in Indochina in 1954 had already shown that empires could be ended, so nationalists in Africa could point to real examples.

The French Union, created by the 1946 constitution, kept the empire under Paris. It was replaced in the 1958 constitution by the French Community, which gave territories internal self-government but left foreign affairs, defence and currency with France.
notes.tip: Keep the French Union (1946) and the French Community (1958) apart. Terms are often tested, so give a definition with the date and say who used it.

notes.b: Before the Algerian war ended, change had already begun elsewhere. Reform in French Africa and independence for Ghana and Guinea showed that independence was becoming possible.
points: The Brazzaville Conference of January–February 1944, a Free French gathering, promised reforms for the empire but ruled out self-government, so it admitted that change was needed while keeping French rule intact.
Tunisia and Morocco, France's neighbours to Algeria's east and west, became independent in March 1956. Their independence mattered to the Algerian war because both later sheltered FLN forces.

The Loi-cadre (framework law) of June 1956, introduced by the minister Gaston Defferre, gave the French African territories elected assemblies and governments with wider powers, an early step towards self-government.

Ghana (the former Gold Coast, a British colony) became independent on 6 March 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, the first sub-Saharan colony to do so, which gave other African nationalists an example to point to.
During an African tour de Gaulle spoke at Brazzaville on 24 August 1958 and offered the territories a choice between the Community and independence.

Guinea, under Sékou Touré, rejected the 1958 constitution (and so the Community) in the referendum of 28 September 1958 and became independent on 2 October 1958, the first French colony in sub-Saharan Africa to leave. Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Tunisia and Morocco had already left French rule.
notes.tip: Ghana (1957, British) and Guinea (1958, French) are easily confused, so tie each to its colonial power and date. For Guinea say first French colony in sub-Saharan Africa, not simply first French colony.

notes.h: 1960: the wind of change and the Year of Africa
notes.b: In 1960 independence came in a rush. A British prime minister gave the movement its best-known phrase, and France's Community broke up in practice.
points: Harold Macmillan, the British prime minister, told the South African Parliament in Cape Town on 3 February 1960 that 'the wind of change is blowing through this continent'.
Seventeen African states became independent in 1960, so it is known as the Year of Africa. Examples include the Ivory Coast, Nigeria and the Congo.

Most French West and Equatorial African territories, along with Madagascar, became independent by negotiation in 1960 and signed co-operation accords with France on defence, currency and aid, so independence did not mean a clean break.
In practice the French Community therefore broke up within two years of its creation, because its members chose independence instead of internal self-government.

Britain chose negotiated transfers of power in most of its colonies. France's policy in Algeria was contested by about a million settlers and an armed nationalist movement, which made a negotiated settlement far harder.
notes.tip: For a paragraph on the winds of change give Ghana 1957, Guinea 1958, Macmillan 1960 and the Year of Africa. Name the speaker, place and year of the Cape Town speech.

notes.b: Algeria was not an ordinary colony in French eyes. It had been conquered long before, was treated as part of France itself, and was home to a large settler community, which is why giving it up was so painful.
points: France began its conquest of Algeria in 1830. By the 1848 constitution Algeria was divided into three départements (administrative districts like those of mainland France) that were treated as part of metropolitan France.

The settlers, known as pieds-noirs, numbered about one million out of about nine million people by 1954. They dominated the economy, land and local administration, so they had much to lose from any change.
The French aim was assimilation: making colonial subjects French in language, law and culture. Few Muslim Algerians accepted this in practice, and most never won full equality.

Most Muslim Algerians were subjects rather than full citizens. Those who wanted full French citizenship had to give up their Islamic personal status (Muslim family law), a condition few chose to meet before 1954.

The Sétif and Guelma uprising of 8 May 1945 killed about 100 Europeans. French repression killed thousands of Algerians: the official French figure is about 1,500, Algerian nationalists claim 45,000, and historians generally accept a figure in between.
Messali Hadj founded the Movement for the Triumph of Democratic Liberties (MTLD) in 1946 to campaign for independence. It split in 1954 between moderates and the armed nationalists.

The Statute of 1947 created an Algerian Assembly with two colleges (voting groups) of equal size. Europeans, with a small number of Muslims, elected the first and the Muslim majority the second, which favoured the settlers because far fewer people elected as many members.
notes.tip: Short questions ask who the pieds-noirs were and why the government could not give in quickly: about a million settlers, with supporters in France, would resist.

notes.h: The FLN rising and the French response, 1954–1957
notes.b: On 1 November 1954 a new nationalist movement chose armed force. France answered with its army, and by 1957 the war was being fought in the cities, the countryside and along the borders.
points: The National Liberation Front (FLN) launched a rising on 1 November 1954 with attacks on police and military targets across Algeria, which began the Algerian war.

The French government sent conscripts (young men called up for compulsory service), reaching about 400,000 troops at the peak. Under Guy Mollet's government in 1956 the Special Powers law gave the army wide powers.
The FLN held the Soummam Valley Congress in August 1956, which set up its political leadership, so the movement had an organised direction beyond its fighting units.
The Morice Line, built from 1957, was a barrier of wire, mines and fencing along the Tunisian border, intended to stop arms and fighters crossing from Tunisia, where the FLN found shelter.

In the Battle of Algiers (January to October 1957) French paratroopers under General Jacques Massu broke the FLN's network in the city through arrests, interrogation and torture. It was a military success won by methods that damaged France's reputation.
notes.tip: A paragraph on the war needs the 1954 rising, the troop numbers, the Battle of Algiers, Massu and torture, and one clear sentence on the results.

notes.b: As the war grew, both sides used methods that shocked observers. How the war was fought turned it into a political problem for France at home and abroad.
points: French forces used torture. Henri Alleg's La Question, an account of his own torture, was banned in France in 1958, but as a first-hand account it brought the issue before French opinion.

Terrorism means violence against civilians to spread fear and win a political aim. The FLN used it, with bombings in Algiers cafés from September 1956 onward, and it also killed Algerian rivals and Muslim opponents.
French forces also killed civilians in reprisal operations (revenge attacks), so civilians suffered at the hands of both sides.

From 1955, and especially after 1957, the French army moved more than a million rural Algerians into fenced regroupement camps as part of its counter-insurgency strategy (the effort to defeat a guerrilla rising).
French military deaths numbered about 25,000. Estimates of Algerian deaths range from about 300,000 to the Algerian official figure of 1.5 million, so historians still debate the figures.
Support for the FLN abroad grew. Tunisia and Morocco sheltered its fighters, Egypt supplied arms, and the UN General Assembly debated Algeria from 1955, so the war was never only a French matter.
On 8 February 1958 French aircraft raided the Tunisian village of Sakiet, which damaged France's reputation with the US and the UN.
notes.tip: Terrorism is often tested. Define it, give the date and say who used it: in Algeria the FLN and, from 1961, the OAS.

notes.h: The May 1958 crisis and de Gaulle's return
notes.b: By 1958 the Fourth Republic could neither win the war nor settle on a policy. A revolt by settlers and army officers in Algiers gave Charles de Gaulle his chance to return to power.
points: Between 1946 and 1958 the Fourth Republic had more than twenty governments, which made it hard to sustain a consistent policy on Algeria and helped bring about its fall.
On 13 May 1958 settlers and army officers seized government buildings in Algiers and demanded that Algeria stay French. They formed a Committee of Public Safety.
The government of Pierre Pflimlin, the last prime minister of the Fourth Republic, lost the confidence of the army, and President René Coty then called on de Gaulle to form a government.
The National Assembly invested de Gaulle on 1 June 1958 as prime minister, not president, because he became president only in January 1959.
Speaking to the crowd in Algiers on 4 June 1958 de Gaulle said 'Je vous ai compris' (I have understood you). At Mostaganem on 6 June he cried 'Vive l'Algérie française'.
These words led the settlers to believe he would keep Algeria French, which is why they later felt betrayed when he changed course.
notes.tip: Do not mix up 1958 and 1959: de Gaulle was prime minister from 1 June 1958 and president from January 1959. Marks go to the sequence with dates, and to explaining why settlers felt betrayed.

notes.h: The Fifth Republic and the Community, 1958–1959
notes.b: De Gaulle's first task was to rebuild the state. The new constitution gave France the strong government the Fourth Republic had lacked, and it set out a new relationship with the colonies.
points: A new constitution was approved by referendum on 28 September 1958, establishing the Fifth Republic with a strong presidency, which gave France stable government after the Fourth Republic's constant changes of government.
The constitution also set up the French Community, which gave the colonies internal self-government but kept foreign affairs, defence and currency with France.
De Gaulle was elected president in December 1958 (on 21 December) by an electoral college, a limited group of electors rather than a popular vote, and he took office on 8 January 1959.

notes.b: Once in office de Gaulle moved step by step away from the settlers' hopes. Each step provoked a violent reaction from those who wanted Algeria to stay French.
points: On 16 September 1959 de Gaulle announced that Algerians would be offered self-determination (the right to decide their own future), with a choice among independence, close association with France and full integration.
Settler militants staged Barricades Week in Algiers from 24 January to 1 February 1960, a revolt against this policy that de Gaulle put down with the army.
Talks with the FLN at Melun in June 1960 failed, so the war went on.
On 4 November 1960 de Gaulle spoke of an Algerian Republic in the future, a clear sign that independence was now a real prospect.

In the referendum of 8 January 1961 about 75 per cent of votes cast overall approved self-determination, and about 70 per cent in Algeria itself, which gave de Gaulle a clear mandate (authority from the voters).

In the Algiers putsch (a seizure of power by force) of 21–26 April 1961, four generals who opposed independence, Challe, Salan, Jouhaud and Zeller, took Algiers. It collapsed in about four days because conscripts and most of the army stayed loyal to de Gaulle.
The Secret Army Organisation (OAS), formed in early 1961 by settlers set on stopping independence, carried out bombings and assassinations in Algeria and in France, and it attacked de Gaulle himself.
notes.tip: Do not merge Barricades Week (settlers, January 1960) with the Algiers putsch (generals, April 1961) or with the May 1958 revolt that brought de Gaulle in.

notes.b: After years of war France and the FLN finally negotiated a settlement. Independence came in stages, which is why several dates are given for it.
points: The Évian Accords were signed on 18 March 1962 after negotiations between the French government and the FLN, and a ceasefire took effect on 19 March.
The Accords guaranteed the rights of the French minority (the settlers), kept the Mers-el-Kébir naval base for France for a time, and gave France access to Saharan oil and gas.
The Accords were approved in a referendum in France on 8 April 1962 (about 91 per cent yes) and in Algeria on 1 July 1962 (an overwhelming yes), so signing them was not the end of the process.
Algeria became independent after the 1 July vote: France recognised it on 3 July, and 5 July is the date celebrated as independence.
After a struggle with rival nationalist leaders in the summer of 1962, Ahmed Ben Bella became prime minister in September 1962 and president in 1963.
notes.tip: Do not give the Évian Accords as the end of the war with no mention of the referendums or the exodus of the settlers.

notes.h: The last OAS violence and its defeat, 1962–1968
notes.b: The OAS tried to wreck the settlement by violence, and the settlers' anger peaked in the weeks after Évian. Its defeat ended the settlers' armed resistance.
points: On 26 March 1962 French troops fired on pro-French demonstrators in the rue d'Isly in Algiers, killing about 50 people, which deepened the settlers' sense of betrayal because the shots came from French soldiers.
The OAS was defeated in Algiers and in France, and its leaders were tried. General Raoul Salan, a leader of the 1961 putsch, was arrested in April 1962 and received a life sentence.

The OAS ambush of de Gaulle's car at Petit-Clamart on 22 August 1962 failed. Its organiser, Jean Bastien-Thiry, was executed in March 1963, the last person executed by firing squad in France for a political offence.
A general amnesty in 1968 freed those OAS members still in prison.
notes.tip: Short questions ask what the OAS did: bombings and assassinations in Algeria and France, and attacks on de Gaulle himself, as at Petit-Clamart.

notes.b: Independence did not end the links between the two countries, but the new state steadily took control of what France had kept.
points: Ben Bella was overthrown by his defence minister Houari Boumediene in June 1965.
France handed over the Mers-el-Kébir naval base in 1968, ending the military presence that the Évian Accords had allowed it to keep for a time.
In 1971 Algeria nationalised (took into state ownership) French oil and gas holdings, reversing the access to Saharan oil and gas that the Accords had given France.

notes.h: The exodus of the pieds-noirs and the harkis
notes.b: Independence turned into flight for the European settlers and tragedy for many of the Algerians who had served France.
points: On 5 July 1962, the day celebrated as independence, violence against Europeans broke out in Oran. Estimates vary, but hundreds were killed or went missing, and many settlers fled the city.
About 800,000 settlers left Algeria in 1962, many within a few months and most for France, which had to absorb them into an already strained economy. Nearly a million had gone by the mid-1960s.
The departure of the settlers ended the French presence in Algerian agriculture and administration, and many farms were taken over by the new state.
The harkis were Algerians who had served as auxiliaries (helpers) in the French forces.
The French government refused or obstructed organised rescue of the harkis, and officers who helped them were punished. About 90,000 reached France with their families.
Tens of thousands of harkis were killed in reprisals (revenge killings) after independence, with estimates ranging widely from about 30,000 to 150,000.

Most harkis who reached France were placed in camps and forest hamlets. Recognition and compensation remained a political issue: President Chirac paid national tribute to them in 2001 and President Macron asked their forgiveness in 2021.
notes.tip: Keep harkis (Muslim auxiliaries) apart from pieds-noirs (European settlers). Short questions ask who the harkis were.

notes.b: De Gaulle led the Free French in the Second World War and then ended the Algerian war as president of the Fifth Republic. His career shows both a leader shaping events and one pushed by them.
points: Born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, he was a career army officer who became undersecretary for war in June 1940. His appeal of 18 June 1940 from London made him leader of the Free French.

He headed the provisional government from 1944 to January 1946, resigned, founded the Rally of the French People (RPF) in 1947, and withdrew from politics in the 1950s before returning to power in 1958.

As the key decision-maker he took the major steps himself: the return in 1958, the Fifth Republic, the 1959 offer of self-determination, putting down Barricades Week and the putsch, and the path to Évian.

In 1958 the settlers welcomed him because they believed he would keep Algeria French, but his 1959 turn showed events shaping him too. He moved from 'Je vous ai compris' in 1958 to self-determination in 1959.
Contemporaries split sharply: the settlers, the army and the OAS called him a traitor, while many in France and Algeria saw him as the leader who ended a costly war.

Some historians argue that he planned withdrawal from early on and moved slowly to avoid civil war. Others argue that he moved step by step as the war's costs, the army's attitude and international pressure became clear.

He used the Community and, after 1960, bilateral co-operation accords (agreements between two countries) to keep French influence in sub-Saharan Africa, working through Jacques Foccart, his adviser on African affairs.
He resigned as president in April 1969 after losing a referendum, and died on 9 November 1970.
notes.tip: For a key personality answer name at least four dated stages: Lille 1890, the 18 June 1940 appeal, Free French, provisional government 1944–46, RPF, return in 1958, Algerian policy and resignation in 1969. Each dated, relevant statement earns marks.

notes.h: Assessment: why France and Britain withdrew from Africa
notes.b: De Gaulle's record and the wider retreat from empire can be judged by pairing achievements against limits, and contemporary views against later ones.
points: Achievement: de Gaulle ended a war that the Fourth Republic had failed to win, and he gave Algerians the right of self-determination.

Limit: the war cost many lives, caused the exodus of about a million people and divided the French army and political class. His policy was also delayed and ambiguous, which left the settlers feeling deceived.
Achievement: the Fifth Republic's constitution gave France a stable government that could take the decision to withdraw.

Limit: the French Community did not hold the colonies together, yet most independent states of West and Equatorial Africa kept close ties with France through co-operation accords, with French troops stationed in several of them.

Explanations for withdrawal: the cost and unpopularity of the Algerian war, the independence of Tunisia and Morocco in 1956, UN General Assembly debates on Algeria from 1955, American pressure, world opinion and the growth of African nationalist parties.
The British and French cases differed: Britain's transfers were mostly negotiated, while France fought a war in Algeria before accepting independence.
Later view: the war divided the army, the political class and French society, and many judge that de Gaulle's greatest achievement was to end it without a collapse of the Republic.
Contemporary view: settlers, the OAS and the generals of the 1961 putsch saw withdrawal as betrayal, while about 91 per cent of French voters approved the Évian Accords in April 1962.
notes.tip: In a Higher essay on de Gaulle and French colonialism, or on why European countries retreated, state a judgement at the start (effective but costly and not entirely by design). Balance achievements against limits with dated evidence, compare French and British experience, and consider both views on whether he planned withdrawal.

keyTerms.definition: The association set up by the 1958 constitution, in which the African colonies had internal self-government while France kept foreign affairs, defence and currency.
The French colonial policy of making colonial subjects French in language, law and culture, which was rarely fully applied in practice.
The use of violence against civilians to create fear and achieve a political aim, used in Algeria by the FLN and by the OAS.
The French settlers of Algeria, about a million people in 1954, most of whom left for France after independence in 1962.
The National Liberation Front, the Algerian nationalist movement that launched the armed rising of 1 November 1954.
The Secret Army Organisation, formed in 1961 by opponents of Algerian independence, which carried out bombings and assassinations.
The agreements of March 1962 between France and the FLN that set out the ceasefire and the terms of Algerian independence.
Harold Macmillan's phrase from his speech in Cape Town in February 1960, describing the wave of African independence.
Algerian Muslims who served as auxiliaries in the French army and were abandoned, killed or settled in camps in France after 1962.
The 1956 French law of Gaston Defferre that gave elected assemblies and wider powers to France's African territories.
The principle that a people may choose its own political status, which de Gaulle offered to Algeria in September 1959.
The French regime founded under de Gaulle by the constitution of 1958, with a strong president.
